content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'liberty' primarily symbolizes the spiritual freedom believers receive in Christ: emancipation from bondage to sin, death, condemnation, and the law as a means of justification. It is freedom for holiness and love, not autonomy or license — the redeemed state of the children of God enabled by the Spirit.","primary_basis":["Galatians 5:1 ('For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery')","Galatians 5:13 ('You were called to freedom... only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh')","John 8:31-36 ('If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed')","2 Corinthians 3:17 ('Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty')","Romans 8:2 ('The law of the Spirit of life has set you free from the law of sin and death')","Romans 8:21 ('the glorious liberty of the children of God')","Romans 6:18-22 (set free from sin, become slaves of righteousness)","Luke 4:18 (Jesus proclaims 'liberty to the captives,' citing Isaiah 61:1)","James 1:25; 2:12 ('the perfect law of liberty')","1 Peter 2:16 ('Live as free people, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Jubilee release — liberty as the Old Testament proclamation of economic and social release (debts forgiven, slaves freed, land returned), read typologically as fulfilled in Christ's ministry and the gospel era.","basis":["Leviticus 25:10 ('Proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants')","Isaiah 61:1-2","Luke 4:18-21 (Jesus applying the Jubilee proclamation to himself)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Christian liberty of conscience — freedom in matters indifferent (adiaphora), i.e., freedom from human religious regulations regarding food, days, and ceremonies, exercised with restraint for the sake of weaker believers. Strongly developed in Reformation theology (e.g., Luther's 'Freedom of a Christian', Westminster Confession ch. 20).","basis":["Romans 14:1-23","1 Corinthians 8:1-13; 10:23-33","Colossians 2:16-23","Galatians 2:4-5"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Socio-political and economic liberation — liberation theology reads biblical liberty as God's action to free the poor and oppressed from unjust structures, taking the Exodus and the Jubilee/Nazareth manifesto as paradigms.","basis":["Exodus 3:7-8; 6:6-7 (deliverance from Egyptian bondage)","Luke 4:18-19","Leviticus 25","Isaiah 58:6"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Civil or national political liberty — reading biblical liberty texts as endorsing constitutional or national freedom (e.g., Leviticus 25:10 on the Liberty Bell; patriotic use of 2 Corinthians 3:17 and Galatians 5:1). Common in popular civil-religious usage but generally rejected by exegetes as the texts' meaning.","basis":["Leviticus 25:10 (as popularly appropriated)","2 Corinthians 3:17 (as popularly appropriated)","Galatians 5:1 (as popularly appropriated)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Liberty as license (libertinism) — a distorted reading, explicitly condemned in the New Testament, that treats freedom in Christ as permission to sin; recognized in interpretation history mainly as the error the epistles warn against.","basis":["Galatians 5:13","1 Peter 2:16","2 Peter 2:19 ('promising them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of corruption')","Jude 4","Romans 6:1-2"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad, cross-traditional agreement (patristic, Catholic, Orthodox, Reformation, and evangelical) that biblical 'liberty' means spiritual freedom from sin, death, and the law's condemnation through Christ, exercised in love and service. The main interpretive divergences concern emphasis rather than the core meaning: Reformation traditions foreground liberty of conscience; liberation theology foregrounds socio-economic liberation; popular civil religion appropriates the term for political freedom, a use most exegetes treat as anachronistic. The Greek term behind most NT uses is eleutheria; 'liberty' and 'freedom' are translation variants of the same concept (KJV favors 'liberty')."}
